notes.meaning: God's people begin their prayer by asking Him to look closely at their deep misery. They know God sees all things, but they are asking Him to step in and act on their behalf. Their greatest sorrow is the public shame brought on them and on the Lord's holy name.
The land of Canaan had been given to God's people long ago as a promised family inheritance. Now foreign invaders have taken over their property, moving into the very houses they had built.
The survivors feel completely alone and unprotected, like children whose fathers have died. Years of war and famine have killed so many men that the land is filled with grieving widows.
The people have lost free access even to the simplest things needed to stay alive. They are now forced to pay their conquerors for drinking water and firewood that used to belong to them.
Cruel enemies ride on the people's necks like a heavy wooden yoke placed on working cattle. The captives are driven hard and forced to work without getting any rest.
To keep from starving, the people had to hold out their hands in surrender to Egypt and Babylon. It was a terrible disgrace for God's chosen nation to beg food from foreign empires just to survive.

Earlier generations lived in rebellion against God and died, leaving the present generation to face the terrible consequences. The survivors mention this long history of sin to ask God for pity, knowing that they too have shared in the nation's guilt.
Former masters and leaders are now ruled by low-ranking servants and foreign soldiers. Being ordered around by petty officials is deeply humiliating, and no human helper is there to set them free.
Gathering basic food has become dangerous because armed desert raiders attack anyone who leaves safety. People have to put their very lives on the line just to gather enough grain to eat.
Extreme hunger has brought on high fevers that scorch the bodies of the people. Their skin has turned dry and withered, looking like an oven heated by flames.
Invading soldiers committed terrible acts of sexual violence against women throughout Jerusalem and Judah. Doing this on holy Mount Zion showed utter contempt for God's sacred dwelling place.
Noble leaders were put to death in cruel ways, hung up by their hands to suffer public disgrace. The invaders showed no respect for the age or wisdom of community elders.
Strong young men were made to do the humiliating work of turning heavy hand-mills like household slaves. Young boys were forced to carry heavy loads of firewood until they collapsed under the weight.
Normal civil life has completely broken down in the ruined city. Wise elders no longer gather at the city gates to guide the community, and young people have stopped playing joyful music.
Deep grief has wiped away all gladness from the hearts of the people. The cheerful dances they once enjoyed during religious festivals have turned into bitter mourning.
The nation has lost its royal dignity, freedom, and former honor. The people openly admit that their own sins brought about this tragic downfall.
The endless sorrow and heavy losses have made the survivors sick at heart. Their eyes have grown blurry and dim from crying so many tears over their crushed city.
Mount Zion, once famous as God's holy dwelling place, now sits empty and ruined. The temple hill is so abandoned by human beings that wild jackals freely walk among the stones.

Although the earthly temple has been torn down, the Lord still sits on His eternal throne in heaven. Earthly kingdoms rise and fall, but God's rule and faithfulness remain steady through every generation.
The people cry out to God, asking why He seems to have left them in pain for so long. They know God does not truly forget His people, but their lengthy suffering makes them feel abandoned.
The mourners beg the Lord to bring them back into His favor so they can be restored. They ask Him to renew their lives and give them the peace and joy they experienced in earlier days.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition often reads this prayer during Holy Week as a call for a soul that has fallen into sin to turn back to God.

notes.meaning: The prayer finishes by asking whether God could really push His people away forever in endless anger. Believers traditionally see this question as a bold plea of faith, trusting that God will never truly break His covenant.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read this verse as facing a real possibility that God had permanently rejected the nation, making restoration impossible.
